1.8 Writable views

Some applications write metadata into the files they show: Photo Mechanic, for example, writes ratings, color labels and flags into JPEGs and DNGs. A read-only disk makes those writes fail. A writable view lets them succeed without touching the source, and passes each written file to the plugin’s written hook, which decides what to keep. Two ways are available.

Shadow file NFS
Enable with "writable": true (disk mode) "mode": "nfs"
Status Ready Experimental
Mounted at /Volumes/LABEL ~/Volumes/LABEL, or mountpoint
Written bytes go to disk.shadow in the session folder overlay/ in the session folder
The plugin sees a write Within about a minute, and on stop About two seconds after the last write, and on stop

Either way, the application reads its own changes back during the session, and diskproxy stop deletes the written bytes after the final capture.

1.8.1 Shadow-file mode

The disk is attached with hdiutil attach -shadow. macOS then treats it as writable, but every changed block goes to the shadow file, and the served image stays read-only. Because the disk delivers blocks rather than files, diskproxy cannot see writes directly. Instead, a harvester process follows filesystem events on the mounted volume, and every minute passes the changed files to the plugin. It reads each file from the mounted volume, so it sees the application’s version.

diskproxy stop asks the harvester for a final pass and waits up to two minutes for it before detaching. If the harvester is not running, stop first walks the whole volume once for files modified since mounting, so no change is lost. If either step fails, the disk stays mounted and stop points at the harvester log.

The harvester can also be run by hand, for example after a crash left a writable volume mounted:

diskproxy-server harvest --config view.json --volume /Volumes/VIEW \
  --since EPOCH --once

--since walks the volume for files modified at or after that Unix time; --once returns after that walk instead of watching. Without --once it keeps watching, every --interval seconds (default 60), until the --stop-file appears. Hidden housekeeping folders such as .fseventsd are skipped.

1.8.2 NFS mode

The first write to a served file copies its presented bytes into the overlay folder; from then on the client reads and writes that copy. New files, new folders, renames and deletions are recorded in the overlay as well, so an application that saves through a temporary file and a rename works normally. Two seconds after the last write to a file, the file is passed to the plugin. When the server receives SIGTERM, which is how diskproxy stop ends it, it passes everything still pending before exiting.
